backontrack-lean-rules.title: BackOnTrack: forward and lateral lean against the rule thresholds, same session
backontrack-lean-rules.desc: The same 48,593-frame, 40.5-minute session, with the firmware's lean features recomputed from the logged quaternion against a neutral taken from the first 10 seconds. Upper panel: forward lean in degrees with the 10 degree Slouching and 25 degree Leaning Forward thresholds; it stays below the Slouching line for 100 percent of frames. Lower panel: lateral lean in degrees with the plus and minus 12 degree Leaning Left and Right thresholds; the wearer sits past the Leaning Left line for 19 percent of the session, one sustained stretch, marked in red.
backontrack-lean-rules.caption: The same session, with the firmware's forward and lateral lean recomputed from the logged quaternion exactly as posture_features.c does, against the thresholds in data_types.h. The device's calibration vector is not in the BLE packet, so the neutral reference is the median gravity direction over the first 10 s of the log. A recomputation, not the classifier's output: forward lean never reaches the 10° line, and lateral lean sits past −12° for 19.3% of frames, one sustained stretch from minute 33.

backontrack-telemetry.title: BackOnTrack: upper-back pitch and EMG over one recorded session
backontrack-telemetry.desc: 48,593 telemetry frames over 40.5 minutes at a median 50 ms frame interval. Upper panel: upper-back IMU pitch in degrees. Lower panel: EMG in millivolts.
backontrack-telemetry.caption: Upper-back pitch (BNO085) and the MyoWare 2.0 signal at the ADC over one 40.5-minute session I wore the device for, from the BLE log in the public repo (tools/bot_20260609_213341.csv). Frames come every 50 ms (20 Hz); the plot draws the min–max band per 7-second window. Only the upper IMU was running, and one calibration-sentinel frame was dropped (48,593 of 48,594 frames plotted). Raw signals, not classifier output. Team project: Sparsh, Matthew, Parneet and Ella.

emg-bci-decoder.title: EMG BCI: what the Kalman decoder does during one reach
emg-bci-decoder.desc: One successful reach toward the +6 target in the zero-lag run, about 6 seconds. Top: the two scaled EMG channels the filter uses as its measurement. Middle: the decoded velocity, pushed up by channel 1 and down by channel 2. Bottom: the cursor position, which integrates the velocity, leaves the center at the go cue, enters the target band at 5.3 to 6.7 units and holds there for half a second until the trial succeeds.
emg-bci-decoder.caption: One successful reach in the zero-lag run, read from its run file: the two scaled EMG channels the filter measures, the decoded velocity and the cursor, with the task phases marked.

emg-bci-lag-sweep.title: EMG cursor BCI: successful reaches and failed center holds versus added feedback lag
emg-bci-lag-sweep.desc: Successful reaches out of 19 attempts, by measured added lag (script setting in brackets): 0 ms (0): 10, about 125 ms (100): 16, about 360 ms (300): 2, about 590 ms (500): 4. Failed center holds: 0 ms: 4, about 125 ms: 5, about 360 ms: 49, about 590 ms: 78. One run per lag condition; the loop ran about 0.12 s instead of the nominal 0.1 s, so the settings of 100, 300 and 500 ms gave about 125, 360 and 590 ms.
emg-bci-lag-sweep.caption: Successful reaches (of 19) and failed center holds at each added feedback lag, counted from the task events in the repo's .mat runs. The loop ran about 120 ms instead of the nominal 100 ms, so the script settings of 100, 300 and 500 ms gave about 125, 360 and 590 ms of added lag. Each lag condition is one run, so the ≈125 ms run beating 0 ms can't be separated from practice or run-to-run effects; the drop from ≈360 ms upward is the effect. Recorded in a three-person EE 466 lab group with Jonathan and Olivia.

emg-bci-loop-timing.title: EMG BCI: the loop ran at about 120 ms, so the real lags were longer than set
emg-bci-loop-timing.desc: Per-loop period in each lag run, 10th to 90th percentile with the median marked, against the nominal 100 ms. Medians: 0 ms run 120 ms, ≈125 ms run 125 ms, ≈360 ms run 119 ms, ≈590 ms run 118 ms. Because lag is set in whole loops (1, 3 and 5), the added lags were about 125, 360 and 590 ms instead of 100, 300 and 500 ms.
emg-bci-loop-timing.caption: Decision 2: per-loop periods from the timing saved in each run (first loop dropped), and the added lag they imply.

emg-bci-session.title: EMG BCI: the recording session on 3 March 2026
emg-bci-session.desc: All five runs were recorded in one session, within about 45 minutes, in this order: zero lag, about 125 ms, about 590 ms, about 360 ms, then position control. 0 ms from 17:18 to 17:21; ≈125 ms from 17:37 to 17:40; ≈590 ms from 17:43 to 17:52; ≈360 ms from 17:55 to 18:01; position from 18:02 to 18:05. The order was not counterbalanced.
emg-bci-session.caption: From each run file's save time and summed loop time. Recorded with my lab group; I was the test subject.

emg-bci-traces.title: EMG BCI: every reach the user saw, by feedback lag and in position control
emg-bci-traces.desc: Displayed cursor position against time from the go cue for all 19 reaches in each run, with the target folded to the top so 6 means on target. 0 ms: 10 of 19 reaches succeeded; ≈125 ms: 16 of 19 reaches succeeded; ≈360 ms: 2 of 19 reaches succeeded; ≈590 ms: 4 of 19 reaches succeeded; position control: 0 of 19 reaches succeeded. At zero and about 125 ms of added lag most reaches settle in the target band; from about 360 ms the cursor overshoots and oscillates, and in position control every reach reaches the target but none holds it.
emg-bci-traces.caption: Every reach in each run, read from the saved Kalman estimates and task events: the cursor as it was displayed (delayed by the run's lag), folded so the target is always up. Recorded with Jonathan and Olivia; I was the test subject.

smartcrib-confusion.title: SmartCrib: confusion matrix of the INT8 model at threshold 0.7
smartcrib-confusion.desc: On the 96 held-out test windows (48 cry, 48 non-cry) the INT8 model found 45 cry windows, missed 3, raised 2 false alarms and classified 46 non-cry windows correctly: recall 93.75%, precision 95.74%, accuracy 94.79%.
smartcrib-confusion.caption: The INT8 model's confusion matrix at threshold 0.7 on the 96 held-out windows, from the repo's selected_threshold.json. The two red cells are the errors: 3 missed cry windows and 2 false alarms.

smartcrib-memory-budget.title: SmartCrib: how much of the Nano 33 BLE Sense the model uses
smartcrib-memory-budget.desc: Against the board's 1 MB flash and 256 KB SRAM: the INT8 model is 7,392 bytes (0.7% of flash); the sketch allocates a 60 KB tensor arena (23.4% of SRAM) of which the INT8 graph is estimated to need 27,648 bytes; the float32 model's estimated arena would have been 56,320 bytes (21% of SRAM). Arena figures are the repo's host-side estimates.
smartcrib-memory-budget.caption: How much of the Nano 33 BLE Sense the model takes: flash use from the INT8 model size, SRAM use from the 60 KB arena the sketch allocates and the repo's estimated arena needs. Arena needs are host-side estimates, not measured on the board.

smartcrib-mfcc-windows.title: SmartCrib: what the model sees, three one-second windows and the INT8 model's answer
smartcrib-mfcc-windows.desc: Three public-dataset clips run through the project's own MFCC pipeline and INT8 TensorFlow Lite model: an infant cry from Donate-a-Cry, a dog bark and a vacuum cleaner from ESC-50. Each column shows the 1-second waveform, the 40-frame by 13-coefficient MFCC input as a heatmap (standardized with the training-set statistics the device uses), and the model's P(cry): 0.9961 for the cry, 0.0547 for the dog bark and 0.0000 for the vacuum cleaner, against the 0.7 operating threshold.
smartcrib-mfcc-windows.caption: Three public-dataset clips run through the project's own MFCC code and INT8 model (re-run from the public repo's scripts and models): a Donate-a-Cry cry, and a dog bark and a vacuum cleaner from ESC-50. Each column is the loudest one-second window of the clip, its 40 × 13 MFCC input standardized the way the device does it, and the model's P(cry) against the 0.7 threshold. Illustrative: these clips come from the training corpora, not the held-out split.

smartcrib-quantization.title: SmartCrib: INT8 quantization shrank model and memory with no accuracy change
smartcrib-quantization.desc: Model size: Keras 58.8 kB, float32 TFLite 12.5 kB, INT8 TFLite 7.4 kB. Tensor arena: float32 56.3 kB, INT8 27.6 kB. Accuracy 94.8% for both on 96 test windows.
smartcrib-quantization.caption: Model size and estimated tensor arena, Keras → float32 TFLite → INT8, from the public repo's reports (model_sizes.csv, metrics_summary.csv). The arena sizes are the repo's estimates. Both TFLite models scored 94.8% accuracy on the 96 held-out test windows. Joint project with Jonathan Lu.

smartcrib-threshold-sweep.title: SmartCrib: threshold sweep on the 96 held-out windows, why 0.7 was picked
smartcrib-threshold-sweep.desc: Cry recall and cry precision of the INT8 TensorFlow Lite model at decision thresholds 0.3 to 0.7 on the 96 held-out test windows, with the float32 model as hollow reference points. Recall is 97.9% at 0.3 to 0.5, 95.8% at 0.6 and 93.75% at 0.7; precision rises from 83.9% at 0.3 to 95.7% at 0.7. The target line is cry recall of at least 0.90; 0.7 is the highest threshold that still meets it, with the fewest false alarms (2 of 48 non-cry windows) and 3 missed cry windows.
smartcrib-threshold-sweep.caption: Cry recall and precision of the INT8 model at each decision threshold on the 96 held-out windows, from the repo's threshold_sweep.csv; hollow points are the float32 model on the same sweep. The dashed line is the 0.90 recall target the threshold had to clear. Joint project with Jonathan Lu.

smartcrib-training-curves.title: SmartCrib: training and validation curves over 12 epochs
smartcrib-training-curves.desc: Accuracy and cross-entropy loss per epoch for the Conv1D model, training (448 windows) against validation (96 windows). Training accuracy rises from 64.7% to 97.5%; validation accuracy from 71.9% to 91.7% at epoch 9 and 10, ending at 89.6%. Validation loss falls from 0.54 to 0.23 by epoch 7 and then flattens while training loss keeps falling to 0.08, the gap that points to some overfitting.
smartcrib-training-curves.caption: Per-epoch accuracy and cross-entropy loss from the repo's training_history.csv: 448 training and 96 validation windows, 12 epochs. Validation loss flattens after epoch 7 while training loss keeps falling, the gap the Results text calls out.

spark-backontrack-pitch.title: BackOnTrack: upper-back pitch over one 40.5-minute session
spark-backontrack-pitch.desc: Median upper-back pitch per 30-second window across the 9 June 2026 logged session (48,593 frames), ranging from 7 to 24 degrees.

spark-emg-reaches.title: EMG BCI: successful reaches by added feedback lag
spark-emg-reaches.desc: Successful reaches out of 19: about 0 ms 10, about 125 ms 16, about 360 ms 2, about 590 ms 4 (higher lags highlighted).

spark-smartcrib-size.title: SmartCrib: model size by format
spark-smartcrib-size.desc: Model size: Keras 58.8 kB, float32 TFLite 12.5 kB, INT8 TFLite 7.4 kB (highlighted).

tpt-chicken-cluster.title: TPT-Finder, BioZ v2: 20 chicken-breast samples at 33 kHz cluster tightly in magnitude and phase
tpt-chicken-cluster.desc: Impedance magnitude against phase at 33 kHz for 167 measurements on 20 ex-vivo chicken-breast samples, measured on the two-electrode BioZ v2 board on 6 November 2025. The 20 per-sample means run from 590.7 to 601.1 ohms (mean 595.5, standard deviation 3.0) and from -6.3 to -4.6 degrees in phase. One reading of 36.6 kilohms was excluded as an outlier.
tpt-chicken-cluster.caption: Redrawn from the poster's Figures II and III using the raw lab file: 167 measurements on 20 ex-vivo chicken-breast samples at 33 kHz, BioZ v2, 6 November 2025. Red dots are the per-sample means; grey dots are the single measurements. One 36.6 kΩ reading was excluded as an outlier.

tpt-liquid-validation.title: TPT-Finder, BioZ v2: impedance and phase of four liquids at 33 kHz
tpt-liquid-validation.desc: Mean ± standard deviation at 33 kHz, measured on the two-electrode BioZ v2 board on 12 February 2026. Distilled water, n = 11: |Z| 207,667 ± 19,990 ohms, phase 45.5 ± 7.8 degrees; Drinking water, n = 15: |Z| 12,294 ± 646 ohms, phase 3.4 ± 0.4 degrees; Gatorade, n = 21: |Z| 616 ± 3 ohms, phase -1.5 ± 0.1 degrees; Saline, n = 10: |Z| 592 ± 0 ohms, phase 6.1 ± 0.0 degrees. Impedance falls by more than two orders of magnitude from distilled water to Gatorade and saline, tracking conductivity.
tpt-liquid-validation.caption: Redrawn from the poster's Figure I using the raw lab files: mean ± SD at 33 kHz on BioZ v2 (two electrodes), 12 February 2026, with n measurements per liquid as printed on the poster. Distilled water, at about 208 kΩ, varies most in both magnitude and phase.

backontrack-bringup.title: BackOnTrack: how the IMU bring-up fault was run down
backontrack-bringup.desc: Six steps. One: both BNO085s return valid part numbers, but calibration fails and every posture value stays at zero. Two: wiring, interrupt and reset lines and the SPI transport are verified, so the hardware is ruled out. Three: comparing against a standalone diagnostic app, iterated six times, shows the diagnostic resets the sensor and drains its boot packets before enabling the Game Rotation Vector report; copying that sequence makes the sensor stream channel-3 reports. Four: values still read zero, so the fault has moved to parsing: wrong feature flags and report ID, fixed on 9 June 2026. Five: the same day the firmware switches to the bundled esp32_BNO08x library. Six: that library is single-instance, which is what left the lower-back IMU disabled.
backontrack-bringup.caption: From my debugging summary (ten phases, condensed to six steps), the repo's debugging/imu_diag project and the commits of 9 June 2026.

backontrack-confirm.title: BackOnTrack: the 750 millisecond confirmation window
backontrack-confirm.desc: A timeline of four seconds. The top row is the raw rule output every frame: Good, then a 400 millisecond Slouching reading at 0.8 seconds while the wearer reaches for something, then Good, then Slouching from 2.0 seconds onward. The bottom row is the reported state: a new state is reported only once the raw output has held it for 750 milliseconds, so the 400 millisecond reach never shows, and the sustained slouch is reported at 2.75 seconds, when the correction alert fires.
backontrack-confirm.caption: Candidate versus reported state in posture_classifier.c: a 400 ms reach never shows, and a sustained slouch is reported 750 ms after it starts. The example timings are illustrative.

backontrack-gravity.title: BackOnTrack: lean measured from the gravity vector, not Euler angles
backontrack-gravity.desc: The BNO085 quaternion gives the direction of gravity in the sensor frame. At calibration the firmware stores that direction as the neutral vector g0 and builds a right axis and a forward axis from it. Each frame it projects the live gravity direction g onto those axes: forward lean is the angle of g in the forward-up plane, lateral lean its angle in the right-up plane, and total lean the angle between g and g0. Everything is a difference from the neutral vector, so the sensor's sign convention and mounting angle drop out. The decomposition holds until the body tilts about 90 degrees from neutral.
backontrack-gravity.caption: How posture_features.c turns the quaternion into forward, lateral and total lean, and the thresholds before and after the 10 June 2026 change.

backontrack-packet.title: BackOnTrack: the 72-byte BLE telemetry packet
backontrack-packet.desc: One packed, little-endian 72-byte notification every 50 milliseconds, 20 per second, on the sensor characteristic. Bytes 0 to 3: uptime in milliseconds. Bytes 4 to 31: the upper IMU as seven floats, pitch, roll, yaw and the quaternion i, j, k, r. Bytes 32 to 59: the same seven floats for the lower IMU, all zero while it is disabled. Bytes 60 to 67: EMG filtered ADC value and millivolts. Byte 68: status flags, bit 0 upper IMU valid, bit 1 lower IMU valid, bit 2 EMG valid, bit 3 calibrated. Byte 69: sequence number, so the receiver can count dropped packets. Bytes 70 to 71: raw EMG ADC. The packet carries raw values only; classification stays on the device.
backontrack-packet.caption: The 72-byte notification the desktop receiver logs to CSV, drawn from ble_telemetry.h in the public repo. Field widths are not to scale.

backontrack-placement.title: BackOnTrack: where the sensors sit on the back
backontrack-placement.desc: Back view of a person. The main module, an ESP32-S3 with the upper BNO085 IMU, sits between the shoulder blades on the strap; it samples the IMU at 50 hertz over SPI. A MyoWare 2.0 EMG sensor sits on the upper trapezius with three gel electrodes and is read by the ESP32-S3's ADC at 100 hertz. A second BNO085 in the lower strap pocket near the lumbar region is part of the team's design and is configured in the firmware, but is disabled at runtime because the bundled driver supports one sensor. Vibration alerts and the companion app over BLE complete the manual's design.
backontrack-placement.caption: Back view, drawn from the team's user manual and the firmware pin map. The lower module is in the design and the code but disabled at runtime (Decision 2). The manual does not say which side of the trapezius; it is drawn on the wearer's right.

backontrack-rules.title: BackOnTrack: the posture rules as a map of forward and lateral lean
backontrack-rules.desc: Left, a map with forward lean on the horizontal axis and lateral lean on the vertical axis, both measured from the calibrated neutral. Forward lean of 25 degrees or more is Leaning Forward; 10 to 25 degrees is Slouching; otherwise lateral lean of minus 12 degrees or less is Leaning Left and plus 12 or more is Leaning Right; otherwise a total lean of 14 degrees or more, for example a diagonal lean or leaning back, is reported as Slouching; the small region inside all of these is Good. Right, the rule order the classifier evaluates on every frame: sensor error gives Unknown; EMG 80 ADC counts above the resting baseline gives High Tension before any angle is checked; a spinal flexion of 12 degrees between the two IMUs would give Lumbar Collapse but needs the disabled lower IMU; then the four angle rules, then Good. A state must hold for 750 milliseconds before it is reported.
backontrack-rules.caption: Every threshold in data_types.h as one map, and the order posture_classifier.c checks them on each frame. Lumbar Collapse is greyed: it needs the disabled lower IMU. Leaning back is caught only by the 14° total-lean rule.

backontrack-system.title: BackOnTrack: wearable posture firmware on an ESP32-S3
backontrack-system.desc: A BNO085 IMU on the upper back over SPI and a MyoWare 2.0 EMG sensor on the ADC feed FreeRTOS tasks and queues on an ESP32-S3. A processing task calibrates, computes posture features, runs a rule-based classifier with good posture plus five fault states, and keeps session statistics. Outputs: a NimBLE GATT packet to a desktop receiver that logs CSV, and serial CSV or JSON telemetry. A second lower-back IMU is configured but disabled at runtime.
backontrack-system.caption: Firmware block diagram, drawn from the public repo's README and source. The lower-back IMU is configured but disabled at runtime.

emg-bci-kalman.title: EMG BCI: the three-state Kalman filter that turns two EMG channels into a cursor
emg-bci-kalman.desc: State: position, velocity and an offset. Each loop the filter predicts with A, in which position gains 0.1 times velocity and velocity decays by a factor of 0.9; process noise is 0.9 on velocity only. The measurement is the two scaled EMG channels, with H mapping channel 1 to plus velocity and channel 2 to minus velocity (in the position-control run, plus and minus position instead), and measurement noise 0.2 per channel. The gain settles to about 0.45 on velocity per unit of channel difference. The update is x equals the prediction plus K times the innovation; the cursor shown is the position from L loops earlier, clamped to plus or minus 10.
emg-bci-kalman.caption: Values as saved in the run files; the gain is the one at the end of the zero-lag run. The decoder settings followed the course protocol.

emg-bci-lag-buffer.title: EMG BCI: the lag buffer
emg-bci-lag-buffer.desc: The decoder makes a new estimate every loop, but the screen shows the estimate from L loops earlier, where L is the set lag divided by the 0.1 second loop period, rounded: 1, 3 or 5 loops for 100, 300 and 500 milliseconds. The loops actually took about 120 milliseconds, so the cursor was about 125, 360 and 590 milliseconds behind the decoder.
emg-bci-lag-buffer.caption: Decision 2: lag is set in whole loops, so the real delay depends on how long each loop actually took.

emg-bci-loop.title: EMG cursor control: closed loop with an added feedback lag
emg-bci-loop.desc: Two EMG channels arrive as a Lab Streaming Layer stream. Every 0.1 seconds MATLAB takes the mean absolute value of each channel, a three-state Kalman filter estimates cursor position, velocity and offset, a lag buffer delays the displayed state by 0, 100, 300 or 500 milliseconds, and the display shows a one-dimensional center-out task. The participant watches the cursor and changes muscle activity, closing the loop.
emg-bci-loop.caption: The closed loop, drawn from the public repo's README and lag-sweep script.

emg-bci-task.title: EMG BCI: the center-out task and how each trial ends
emg-bci-task.desc: The display is one-dimensional, from minus 10 to plus 10 units, with a center target and two peripheral targets at plus and minus 6, each 0.7 units in radius. Each trial waits 0.5 seconds, then the cursor must hold in the center for 0.5 seconds; leaving early is a failed center hold (code 9) and the trial restarts. At the go cue the user has 5 seconds to reach the target (otherwise a reach timeout, code 8), then must hold it for 0.5 seconds (leaving early is a target-hold failure, code 10). Only a reach that holds counts as a successful reach. A run has 20 trials, 10 to each target.
emg-bci-task.caption: The task as the lag-sweep script defines it; targets, hold times, limits and error codes are read from the saved run files.

shield-bias-sweep.title: Project SHIELD: the 81-step bias-injection sweep
shield-bias-sweep.desc: The firmware sequencer I wrote runs 81 bias-injection sessions from one boot: 3 trials, each covering 9 axes at 3 severities. Bias values are registers the sequencer sets per step; an NVS checkpoint after each step makes the sweep resume-safe after a power cycle, and every run writes a b4_meta.json sidecar with its axis, severity, trial, step index, status and firmware commit.
shield-bias-sweep.caption: Decision 3: what my firmware sequencer runs from a single boot.

shield-fault-map.title: Project SHIELD: faults, stress sessions and the rigs that run them
shield-fault-map.desc: From the capstone poster's Fault Injection panel: software faults to inject are bias, drift, burst noise, dropouts, stuck-at, clipping and latency; hardware faults are power variation, EMI or analog noise, and bus disturbance; the goal is to compare fault behaviour against the nominal baseline and produce a labelled dataset for fault detection and machine learning. In the ARC Lab stress campaign, bias injection runs on my 81-step firmware sequencer, vibration sessions run on the orbital shaker driven by my PC scripts, EMI sessions use the Faraday cage I designed and built, and thermal sessions use the team's setup.
shield-fault-map.caption: The poster's fault list, and the rig behind each stress session in the ARC Lab campaign. Red tags mark the parts I built.

shield-freertos.title: Project SHIELD: the dual-core FreeRTOS acquisition pipeline
shield-freertos.desc: Redrawn from the capstone poster's Figure 2. On core 0, three acquisition tasks poll the sensors in three tiers: FastTask at priority 10 runs a 1 millisecond loop for the BNO085 accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer, the SW-420 and the INMP441 (1 kHz); MediumTask at priority 8 runs a 5 millisecond loop for the ACS723 current sensor and the photodiode through the ADS1115 (200 Hz); SlowTask at priority 6 runs a 20 millisecond loop for the MPL3115A2 pressure and MCP9808 temperature sensors (50 Hz). Each task pushes records into its own FreeRTOS queue. On core 1, a single SDWriter task at priority 5 drains the three queues into 16 KB per-file buffers, flushes every second or when a buffer is full, and updates the metadata every 60 seconds, writing fast_data.bin, medium_data.bin, slow_data.bin, meta.json and events.log to a run folder on the microSD card. A live streamer sends the data over USB serial to pc_viewer.py on the PC. Every stored sample is written as raw plus processed 20-byte V2 records.
shield-freertos.caption: Redrawn from the capstone poster's Figure 2. The acquisition firmware is the team's; my commits extend it.

shield-ml-pipeline.title: Project SHIELD: the team's machine-learning pipeline design
shield-ml-pipeline.desc: Redrawn from the capstone poster's Figure 5. Raw sensor telemetry is cut into fixed-length windows and labelled using synthetically injected faults with randomized onsets and severities; each window becomes a feature vector of time-domain statistics, frequency-domain spectral features and wavelet coefficients; classification models are trained to tell healthy sensor behaviour from fault conditions. The requirements set the final target: predict a failure at least 20 seconds before functional loss.
shield-ml-pipeline.caption: Redrawn from the poster's Figure 5: the team's ML pipeline design. Model training is ongoing.

shield-shaker-campaign.title: Project SHIELD: the four-session shaker campaign
shield-shaker-campaign.desc: Four back-to-back 70-minute sessions at low, medium, medium and high speed, 280 minutes in all. Each session is 5 minutes settling with the shaker off, 60 minutes at the target speed and 5 minutes of recovery. One button press on the board arms the first session; after that the board follows the PC script's zero-gap chaining for sessions 2 to 4. The A1 protocol's speeds are 80, 140 and 200 RPM.
shield-shaker-campaign.caption: Decision 4: one button press arms the first session; the PC script chains the other three.

shield-system.title: Project SHIELD: system diagram of the DAQ board
shield-system.desc: Redrawn from the capstone poster's Figure 1. A 9 volt battery feeds a 9 to 5 volt converter; 5 volts powers the ESP32-S3 board, the microSD module and the current sensor, and the ESP32-S3 supplies 3.3 volts to the other modules. Inside the ESP32-S3, raw sensor data is scaled and converted, tagged with metadata (sensor type, unit ID, model, sampling rate, timestamp reference and run ID) and buffered. The sensor modules, tested one at a time on five units each, are an IMU (BNO085, SPI: accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer), a pressure sensor (MPL3115A2, I2C), a temperature sensor (MCP9808, I2C), a microphone (INMP441, I2S), a photodiode and a current sensor (ACS723) read through an ADS1115 analog-to-digital converter on I2C, and a vibration switch (SW-420, GPIO). Data goes to a microSD card over SPI as binary sensor files plus JSON metadata, and to a host PC over USB serial; a Wi-Fi web view exists but is compiled off by default.
shield-system.caption: Redrawn from the capstone poster's Figure 1 (team design).

smartcrib-pipeline.title: SmartCrib: training pipeline and on-device cry detection
smartcrib-pipeline.desc: Offline: Donate-a-Cry cry clips and ESC-50 negatives become 40-frame by 13-coefficient MFCC features, train a compact Conv1D model, which is quantized to an 7.4 kB INT8 TensorFlow Lite model, and a threshold sweep picks 0.7 to meet a 0.90 recall target. On device: an Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense records from its PDM microphone, computes MFCCs for each one-second window, runs the INT8 model, applies the threshold and a three-window majority vote, and raises a GPIO alert to an ESP32 bridge that sounds a buzzer and exposes a BLE alert.
smartcrib-pipeline.caption: Training pipeline (offline) and on-device detection (Nano 33 BLE Sense → ESP32 alert bridge), drawn from the public repo's README and source.

smartcrib-tflite-ops.title: SmartCrib: why the Conv1D model was rebuilt as a Conv2D-equivalent graph
smartcrib-tflite-ops.desc: The standard Conv1D export wraps each convolution in EXPAND_DIMS operations, which the Arduino TensorFlowLite 2.4.0-ALPHA library does not support. The converter was rebuilt to emit a graph of six supported operators with the same trained weights: input 40 by 1 by 13, CONV_2D with a 3 by 1 kernel and 16 filters, MAX_POOL_2D, CONV_2D with 32 filters, MEAN (global average pooling), FULLY_CONNECTED to two classes and SOFTMAX. Operator list and shapes read from the INT8 .tflite file.
smartcrib-tflite-ops.caption: The Conv1D export that failed and the six-operator graph that replaced it, with the kernel sizes and tensor shapes read from the INT8 .tflite file in the public repo.

tpt-finder-electrodes.title: TPT-Finder: two-electrode BioZ v2 versus four-electrode BioZ v4
tpt-finder-electrodes.desc: Left, BioZ v2: two electrodes on the tissue. E1 is driven by the AD8606 buffer and E2 returns the current to the AD8606 transimpedance stage, so the reading includes the contact impedance at both electrodes in series with the tissue. Right, BioZ v4: four electrodes. The outer pair injects the current (driven by the AD8606 buffer) and returns it to ground; the inner pair senses the voltage through an INA333 instrumentation amplifier with a gain of about 1000 and its reference at 1.65 volts, into the AD5933. The sense electrodes carry almost no current, so their contact impedance stays out of the measured voltage.
tpt-finder-electrodes.caption: Why BioZ v4 moved to four electrodes. The v2 wiring is read from its KiCad netlist; the v4 wiring is from the March 2026 design worklog for the four-port redesign.

tpt-finder-signal-chain.title: TPT-Finder: the BioZ v2 two-electrode measurement chain
tpt-finder-signal-chain.desc: A Python GUI on a laptop talks over USB to an ESP32 running ESP-IDF firmware with the AD5933 I2C driver. On the BioZ v2 board, the AD5933 impedance converter, clocked by a 16 MHz oscillator, sends its excitation from VOUT through a 47 nF coupling capacitor, biased to mid-supply by a 49.9 kilohm divider, into channel A of an AD8606 wired as a unity buffer, which drives electrode E1. The current through the tissue returns on electrode E2 into channel B of the AD8606, a transimpedance stage with 49.9 kilohm feedback, then through a 20 kilohm input resistor (20 kilohm RFB) into the AD5933's VIN, where an on-chip DFT gives the real and imaginary parts. The same electrode pair drives and senses, so electrode contact impedance is part of every reading. Calibration against a 2200 ohm reference reached 0.034 percent error at 33 kHz.
tpt-finder-signal-chain.caption: The BioZ v2 measurement chain, which took the poster data, read from the board's KiCad netlist. The same electrode pair drives and senses.
